d.title: One outlier of 999, and what each scaler does with it
d.caption: The fee column runs 6.43 to 19.99 with one value of 999. Watch the three plans' rows: under **min-max** they are crushed into 0.002 to 0.014, because the range is defined by the outlier and every real customer now occupies 1% of the scale. Under **standardisation** they sit at −0.14 to 0.24, because the outlier owns the mean (12.49) and the standard deviation (31.65). Only **robust** scaling, which uses the median and IQR, leaves the real customers spread from −0.47 to 1.81 — and it puts the outlier at 187.6, where it is impossible to miss.

d.title: Which algorithms care about scale, and why
d.caption: The reason is always the same shape: something in the objective sums across features with one coefficient. A distance adds squared differences; one λ penalises every weight equally; one learning rate steps every input. A tree compares one feature with one constant and never adds anything across columns — so any monotone rescaling gives identical splits.
cells: the widest column dominates the distance
one lambda penalises every weight equally
one step size for every input
the optimum is unit-free; conditioning is not
a split is one feature against a constant
each feature is modelled on its own

d.title: A scaler is a fitted object, and where it is fitted is the whole question
d.caption: A scaler learns two numbers from the rows it is shown. Fit it on everything and those numbers carry the test rows' mean and range into the training data — a mild leak, but a leak that is free to avoid. The sparse exception is worth knowing: centring a sparse matrix fills in every zero, so `with_mean=False` keeps the sparsity and scales by the standard deviation only.

d.title: One-hot, and the trap that only bites some models
d.caption: k levels become k columns that sum to 1 in every row, so with an intercept the design matrix is singular — the dummy-variable trap. It matters for an unpenalised linear model, where coefficients become arbitrary, and it does **not** matter for a tree or a penalised model. Dropping a level fixes the collinearity and makes every coefficient a comparison against that level, which is why the choice of baseline changes what the numbers mean.

nodes.label: 4 one-hot columns
nodes.sub: they sum to 1 in every row

d.title: Ordinal encoding invents an order, and a line believes it
d.caption: The true effects on the logit are red +2.0, green −1.0, blue +2.5, yellow −2.0 — no order at all. The encoder sorts them alphabetically and hands the model blue 0, green 1, red 2, yellow 3, which asserts blue < green < red < yellow. A logistic regression has to fit a single straight line through +2.5, −1.0, +2.0, −2.0 and scores **0.785**; one-hot scores 0.972. A tree is untouched: it splits the integer at 0.5, 1.5 and 2.5 and recovers every level in three splits, because it never assumed the order was real.

d.title: Two thousand cities: what one-hot costs and what replaces it
d.caption: At high cardinality one-hot is not merely wide — most columns have too few ones to estimate anything from, so the model is fitting noise in two thousand places. Each alternative collapses the column to one or a few, and each pays for it differently.

d.title: The mechanism decides what is safe to do
d.caption: Under MNAR the value's own size is what caused it to be absent — high earners declining to state income — so every imputer fills in a typical value for rows that are systematically atypical. No imputation recovers the values; an indicator column recovers the **fact**, which is often the stronger feature.
cells: impute from them, plus an indicator
indicator first; no imputer recovers it

d.title: Row deletion scored best and would have been the worst decision
d.caption: The 126 customers with no tickets field churn at 0.222 against 0.154 — dropping them raised the AUC because the **remaining problem is easier**, not because the model improved. The deployed model meets those customers on day one, with no tickets value, and still has to score them. A treatment is judged on the population the model will serve.

the fills would be mostly fiction

d.title: MNAR, planted: the indicator recovers what no imputer can
d.caption: Twenty-seven of the forty-one rows with three or more tickets were hidden — so the gaps are the **angriest customers**, churning at 0.333 against 0.148 for the rest. Median imputation hands each of them a ticket count of 1, which is exactly the wrong value, and loses ground against the complete column. Iterative imputation predicts a typical value from the other columns and is still wrong by design. Adding the indicator recovers 0.766 either way: the model does not need the value, it needs to know the row was hidden.

d.title: A categorical imputer is a fitted step, and the fold is where it belongs
d.caption: Filling a categorical with its mode, or with a literal 'missing' level, is a choice with consequences: the mode hides the gap inside an existing level, while a 'missing' level lets the model learn from absence directly — which is what a NaN-native booster does for you, by sending missing rows to whichever child reduces the loss.

d.title: A log transform made the skew worse, and a fitted power fixed it
d.caption: Spend has skew +0.59 and a hard zero. `log1p` takes it to **−2.06** — worse, and in the other direction, because it stretches the zeros and near-zeros into a long left tail. A fitted Box-Cox finds λ = 0.644, between a square root and no transform at all, and lands on +0.03. The lesson generalises: `log1p` is the right bend for a **count** with many zeros (tickets, skew 0.93 to 0.32) and the wrong one for a continuous amount with a floor.

d.title: Nine shapes of derived feature, and who needs them
d.caption: The last column is the part worth internalising: most of these exist to give a **linear or distance** model something it cannot construct itself. A tree can already find a threshold interaction by nesting two splits, so generic polynomial expansion mostly adds width and noise there.

d.title: Three ways to let a straight line bend
d.caption: A linear model's coefficient is one number for the whole range, which asserts the effect is constant. Each of these buys a different kind of flexibility: bins give a step function and discard resolution inside each step, splines bend smoothly where the knots are, and a cyclical pair makes midnight adjacent to 23:00 instead of twenty-three hours away.

d.title: Find, then decide — and they are separate steps
d.caption: Detection is a statistical question with several answers; what to do about it is a domain question with only one source of truth. Collapsing them is how a genuine extreme value — the bulk order, the record day — gets winsorised into a plausible-looking lie.

d.title: Fifty-one features, six of them real, and why selection pays
d.caption: The bench: five linear signals, one U-shaped signal, three linear combinations of the first three, two near-duplicates, and forty columns of pure noise. A logistic regression on **all 51** scores 0.867; on the true six it scores **0.875** — fewer features, a better score, because the 45 extra columns cost variance without adding signal. The forest reaches 0.909 on all 51, because it can use the U-shape a logistic regression cannot and barely notices the noise.

d.title: What each selector can and cannot see
d.caption: The two columns that decide most choices: whether the test can see a **non-linear** relationship at all, and what it does with correlated copies. An F-test ranks every copy of a useful feature highly; lasso picks one of them arbitrarily; permutation importance shares the credit, so a correlated copy can hide the drop entirely.

d.title: What each method actually picked, on a bench where the truth is known
d.caption: Six features requested; the true six are inf0–inf4 and nonlin. **Forward sequential selection chose two noise columns** — greedy search on noisy CV folds overfits the search itself. RFE dropped inf0 and let its correlated copies stand in for it. Lasso kept nine, including three noise columns. And the forest's importance spread inf0's credit across inf0, red0 and dup0 (0.062 + 0.077 + 0.064), which is why a single importance number understates a feature that has copies.

state: 5 right; red0 and dup0 for inf0

d.title: Where selection must run
d.caption: Selecting on all the rows means the choice of columns was informed by the rows you later score — and with more features than rows you can select pure noise and get a convincing cross-validated number out of it. The selector is a fitted step like any other.

d.title: The contract every transformer keeps
d.caption: Three methods and one rule: nothing is learned until `fit`, and everything learned is stored in an attribute ending in an underscore. Before `fit`, a scaler has no such attributes at all — which is exactly why a pipeline can be cloned per fold and refitted without leaking anything between them.

d.title: One ColumnTransformer, three branches, one fitted object
d.caption: Columns are selected **by name**, so a reordered input cannot silently shift the pipeline, and `remainder='drop'` means a new column added upstream is excluded rather than fed in unseen. Each branch is itself a small pipeline, and the whole assembly is one estimator that cross-validation can clone — which is what makes every leakage rule in module 1 automatic rather than remembered.

d.title: A custom transformer that keeps the contract
d.caption: The rule that makes it safe: anything derived from the data is computed in `fit` and stored with a trailing underscore; `transform` only applies it. A transformer that computes a median inside `transform` recomputes it on the test fold — which is a leak in the other direction, and one that cross-validation will not catch because each fold looks self-consistent.
